questions.knowledge_point: Identifying and Interpreting the Lotka-Volterra Model
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-3x+4xy \\ {y}^{′}=2y-xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above for the functions $x(t)$ and $y(t).$ Select the correct options in the following statement.$\,$
Term ${y}^{′}$ in the second equation represents the 
{{field-1}} 
of the 
{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants. 

First, recall that a derivative represents a $\text{rate of change}.$

For the ${y}^{′}$ equation, we have

$$
{y}^{′}=2y-xy.
$$

Therefore, $y$ must represent the $\text{prey}.$ Indeed, 

- it grows exponentially in the absence of predators (the $2y$ term), and

- decreases when interacting with predators (the $-xy$ term).

questions.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of the Lotka-Volterra System
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-2x+5xy \\ {y}^{′}=7y-3xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.

$(${{field-1}}
$,$
{{field-2}}$)$
questions.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system ${x}^{′}(t)=f(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=0.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-2x+5xy=0 \\ 7y-3xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+5xy & =0 \\ x(-2+5y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\frac{2}{5}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-3(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\frac{2}{5},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}7y-3xy & =0 \\ y(7-3x) & =0 \\ \frac{2}{5}(7-3x) & =0 \\ 7-3x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $(\frac{7}{3},\frac{2}{5}).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$(\frac{7}{3},\frac{2}{5}).$

questions.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model
questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=0.7x-0.35xy \\ {y}^{′}=-0.4y+2xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0.2,\,2]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=0.7x-0.35xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-0.4y+2xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(0.7x-0.35xy)=0.7-0.35y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(0.7x-0.35xy)=-0.35x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4y+2xy)=2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4y+2xy)=-0.4+2x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}0.7-0.35y & -0.35x \\ 2y & -0.4+2x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0.2 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}0.7-0.35(2) & -0.35(0.2) \\ 2(2) & -0.4+2(0.2)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & -0.07 \\ 4 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & -0.07 \\ 4 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-4\cdot (-0.07) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.28 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\pm 0.2\sqrt{7}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is $\text{a stable}$ $\text{center}.$

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).

questions.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=4x-2xy \\ {y}^{′}=-3y+5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the prey and $y=y(t)$ represents the predators. Select the correct options in the reasoning below.$\,$ Evaluating the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\,0]^{T},$ we get

| $J({x}^{∗})=\,\,$ |  | {{field-1}} | {{field-2}} |  | $\,.$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | {{field-3}} | {{field-4}} |  |  |  |

$\,$ The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are 
{{field-5}}.

$\,$ Therefore, the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}$ is 
{{field-6}}{{field-7}}.
questions.worked_solution:
Let's denote ${f}_{1}(x,y)=4x-2xy$ and ${f}_{2}(x,y)=-3y+5xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-2xy)=4-2y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x-2xy)=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y+5xy)=5y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y+5xy)=-3+5x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is

$$
J=[\begin{aligned}4-2y & -2x \\ 5y & -3+5x\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
J({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}4-2(0) & -2(0) \\ 5(0) & -3+5(0)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

The eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix are ${\lambda }_{1}=4\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=-3.$ Since eigenvalues are real with opposite signs, our equilibrium is $\text{an unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Identifying and Interpreting the Lotka-Volterra Model
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-8x+2xy \\ {y}^{′}=4y-xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above for the functions $x(t)$ and $y(t).$ Provide an interpretation of each equation in the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The Lotka-Volterra predator-prey model is given by

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=ax-bxy \\ {y}^{′}=-cy+dxy\end{aligned}
$$

where $a,b,c,d$ are positive real constants. 

First, recall that a derivative represents a rate of change.

For the $x'$ equation, we have

$$
x' = -8x + 2xy.
$$

Therefore, $x$ must represent the predator. Indeed,

- it decays exponentially in the absence of prey (the $-8x$ term), and

- increases when interacting with prey (the $2xy$ term).

For the $y'$ equation, we have

$$
y' = 4y - xy.
$$

Therefore, $y$ must represent the prey. Indeed, 

- it grows exponentially in the absence of predators (the $4y$ term), and

- decreases when interacting with predators (the $-xy$ term).

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Finding Equilibrium Points of the Lotka-Volterra System
canonical_examples.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-4x+7xy \\ {y}^{′}=9y-5xy\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey. Find the nonzero equilibrium of the model.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equilibrium (fixed) points of a system $\mathbf{x}'(t) = \mathbf{f}(x,y)$ are the points for which $f(x,y)=\mathbf{0}.$ So, we get the following system of linear equations:

$$
{\begin{aligned}-4x+7xy=0 \\ 9y-5xy=0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-4x+7xy & =0 \\ x(-4+7y) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $x=0$ or $y=\dfrac{4}{7}.$ We consider both cases separately.

- If $x=0,$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-5(0)y=0\,⇒\,y=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, one equilibrium is $(0,0).$

- If $y=\dfrac{4}{7},$ substituting it into the second equation, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}9y-5xy & =0 \\ y(9-5x) & =0 \\ \frac{4}{7}(9-5x) & =0 \\ 9-5x & =0 \\ x & =\frac{9}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, another equilibrium is $\left(\dfrac{9}{5}, \dfrac{4}{7}\right).$

Therefore, the nonzero equilibrium of the model is
$\left( \dfrac{9}{5}, \dfrac{4}{7} \right).$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Classifying Equilibria of the Lotka-Volterra Model
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the Lotka-Volterra model above, where $x=x(t)$ represents the predators and $y=y(t)$ represents the prey.

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}=-0.4x+0.4xy \\ {y}^{′}=y-4xy\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the Jacobian of the system at the equilibrium point $\mathbf{x^\ast}=[0.25, \, 1]^T,$ and classify this equilibrium point.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let's denote $f_1(x,y)=-0.4x+0.4xy$ and $f_2(x,y)=y-4xy.$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=-0.4+0.4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-0.4x+0.4xy)=0.4x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-4xy)=-4y,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-4xy)=1-4x\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the Jacobian matrix is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/e526dd9bda292c2a25920b8248820f3ed88c0bc4c4a55e3ba3f2db925af486d8.png)

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/cc6e0f2742f419fc8f2c09bf69c97f72d7e7f1ca0d98c3845996e216849f4316.png) to get

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14094872/assets/bcc787d9cceae4a7280c6af84c0d7bf95c15dfc90cf9e3bdedf2a52362c1b225.png)

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-\lambda  & 0.1 \\ -4 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-\lambda )(-\lambda )-(-4)\cdot 0.1 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+0.4 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm 0.2\sqrt{10}\,\text{i}.$ Since the eigenvalues are purely imaginary, our equilibrium is a stable center.

**Note:**
For the Lotka-Volterra model (as in this problem), it is safe to classify the nonzero equilibrium as a center when the linearization has purely imaginary eigenvalues. 

**Watch out!** 
In contrast, for a general nonlinear system, the Jacobian test alone is inconclusive (additional analysis is required to determine whether the equilibrium is a true center or a spiral sink/source).
